## What the law says

- **Minimum standard:** The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Version 004, in force 1 July to 24 November 2025) say that "each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This is clause 8 of Schedule 4, so the test is mould linked to the building structure, not any mould at all.
- **Provider's duty:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Version 110, in force 6 August to 24 November 2025) requires the provider to ensure rented premises comply with the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the renter moves in. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Advertising:** The advertising rule, section 65B, which bars advertising premises unless the provider or agent "reasonably believes the premises comply with the rental minimum standards," appears in the later Version 111 (in force from 25 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Version 110 text I retrieved does not include section 65B, so I can't confirm that the advertising rule applied on 1 October 2025. The 65B penalties are 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## What the renter can do or ask

- If the premises don't meet the standards when the renter moves in, the renter "may issue a request to the residential rental provider for urgent repairs" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The provider must also keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation," whether or not the renter knew of the disrepair beforehand [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If the renter has not yet moved in, a provider who fails to deliver the premises in the required condition can cause the renter to owe no rent for the period before they move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). That provision refers to premises being "vacant" and "in a reasonably clean condition," not to mould specifically [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't answer

- **Whether the photo proves non-compliance:** None of the retrieved documents addresses how much weight a photo carries as evidence. Later record-keeping duties for advertised premises appear in Version 115 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), which is not in force on 1 October 2025.
- **Whether the advertisement itself was unlawful on 1 October 2025:** As noted above, the retrieved Version 110 text doesn't show section 65B.

If you need a firm answer on the photo question or on the advertising rule for 1 October 2025, you would need the full Version 110 Act text and guidance from Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

**Short answer:** Based on the documents, the notice has not been withdrawn, so it has not ended on its own. But the documents don't say whether a sale notice stays enforceable after the sale falls through. You should get advice before deciding what to do.

## What the law says

- **Governing version:** For 1 October 2025, the applicable Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **No. 110**, in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Later versions (No. 111, from 25 November 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf); No. 115, from 13 October 2026 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)) don't apply on that date.
- **Sale notices:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession." The termination date must be at least **60 days** after the notice is given. If there is a contract of sale subject to conditions, the notice must be given within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. If there is an unconditional contract, it must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." That notice must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Silence or a change of plans doesn't withdraw it.
- **Enforcement:** A landlord can't evict you directly. If you don't leave by the termination date, the landlord may apply to VCAT for a possession order. VCAT decides whether the landlord was entitled to give the notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant for possession [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord in writing** to sign a notice of withdrawal. Under s 91ZZQ, this is the only way the notice is formally withdrawn [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the deadline to challenge the notice.** You may apply to VCAT challenging the notice's validity, on or before the hearing of a possession order application. The application must be made within **30 days after the notice to vacate is given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This deadline may already be close or past, so check the date on your notice now.
3. **Consider the validity grounds.** The notice must be in the prescribed form and accompanied by documentary evidence supporting the reason given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 6 also says a notice can be challenged if you believe it was not given to you properly, or if the information in it is incorrect or incomplete [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **Know the protections.** A landlord who obtains possession after a sale notice generally can't re-let the premises for use as a residence within 6 months of the notice, subject to exceptions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
5. **Get urgent advice.** Form 6 advises seeking advice immediately from community legal organisations listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, or calling 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether a sale notice remains valid after the sale collapses, or whether the landlord must then rely on a different ground. The retrieved documents don't address this.
- The date your notice was given and its termination date. Both are needed to check the 30-day and 60-day limits.

### What the law says

- **A valid notice is required.** "A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice must be in the prescribed form and give at least 60 days' notice.** On 1 October 2025, the provider "must give a renter at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **The notice must contain specific details.** It must include "the amount of the rent increase," "the method by which the rent increase was calculated," and a statement of your right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The prescribed form is Form 5 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Only one increase per notice, and no more than once every 12 months.** A notice "may only provide for one rent increase" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), and rent cannot be increased "at intervals of less than 12 months" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Increases made in breach are invalid.** "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

A refusal to negotiate is not a notice, so it does not start the 60-day period. I can't see the agent's email, so I can't say whether it contains the required content. However, you say you have not received an official notice.

### What you can do or ask

- **Ask for a Form 5 notice.** If the increase is genuine, the provider must give you a notice meeting the requirements above. Check that it states the new amount, the start date, and the calculation method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the start date.** The Form 5 notice has a "Start date" field [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), and the statute requires at least 60 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). An increase cannot take effect before that period has run.
- **Challenge it if it's excessive.** Within 30 days after the notice is given, you can apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate and report on the proposed rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You can also apply to VCAT within 30 days after receiving the Director's report, or within 30 days of the notice if there is no report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You would need to satisfy VCAT that you have reasonable grounds to apply without first getting a Director's report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Note the payment rule if you challenge.** If you apply to VCAT, you will need to pay the increased amount from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Version 111 of the Act, in force from 25 November 2025, changes the notice period to 90 days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents do not specify a start date for an increase where no valid notice has been given, so no lawful increase date can be identified from these facts. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Also, rent generally cannot be increased more than once every 12 months, and it cannot be increased during a fixed term unless the agreement allows it. If the stated reason was that the premises needed repairs, the rental provider had to intend to repair, renovate or reconstruct the premises, have all necessary permits and consents, and be unable to do the work properly unless you vacated. The notice also had to give at least **60 days’ notice** and be accompanied by supporting documentary evidence. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What the law says on 1 October 2025

- **Governing versions:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 Authorised Version No. 110 was in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). - **Mould standard:** Schedule 4 of the Regulations states: "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to comply:** The Act requires the provider to ensure rented premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Advertising:** Version 110 of the Act does not show a section 65B on advertising premises that don't meet the standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). That provision first appears in Version 111, which is in force from 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). It says a provider or agent must not advertise premises unless they "reasonably believe" the premises comply with the minimum standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). So on 1 October 2025, the retrieved documents don't show that rule in force, and I can't confirm from them when it started.

## Is the photo enough to prove a breach?

The documents don't answer this directly. The mould standard covers mould "caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), and a photo shows that mould is present but not its cause. The documents also don't set out a test for what evidence proves non-compliance. The only related guidance is that photos "may be useful in a dispute about the condition of the rented premises" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo is evidence, but the documents don't say whether it is enough on its own.

**Which version applies:** On 1 October 2025, the applicable document is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110, in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Version 111 starts on 25 November 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and version 115 starts on 13 October 2026 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so I haven't relied on either.

**What the law says**

- **Basis for the notice:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date. If a contract of sale is conditional, the notice must be given within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. If the contract is not conditional, it must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given. That notice must be in writing and signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Nothing in the retrieved text says a notice is withdrawn automatically when a sale falls through.
- **Possession order:** The landlord may apply to the Tribunal for a possession order after the notice is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must be satisfied that the notice has not been withdrawn, and that a possession order is reasonable and proportionate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal cannot decide the application before the termination date in the notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for a withdrawal:** You can ask the landlord to sign a written notice of withdrawal. Under the Act, it only takes effect if you also sign it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The landlord is not required to sign it.
2. **Challenge the notice:** For a sale notice, you may apply to the Tribunal challenging its validity. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If that window has passed, the documents don't say whether a challenge is still possible. Check when the notice was given.
3. **Respond to a possession application:** If the landlord applies for a possession order, the Tribunal decides whether it is reasonable and proportionate to make one [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You can attend the hearing.

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether a sale notice stays valid after the contract falls through, or whether the landlord must still intend to sell.
- Your termination date, whether your agreement is fixed-term, and when the notice was given. These details affect the answer.

This is general information from the Act, not legal advice. Given the 30-day deadline, I would seek tenant advice promptly.

- The notice can only provide for one rent increase, and must include the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and a statement of your right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

- The prescribed form is Form 5 in the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version 004, in force 1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025). It states that "a valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" and that the rental provider "must not increase the rent more than once every 12 months" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Form 5 also says the rental provider's name "cannot be the agent's name," and that notice by email is only valid if the renter has consented to email [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

From 25 November 2025, the notice period became 90 days, in both the Act [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the Regulations (Form 5) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm from the documents whether an email from an agent could ever meet this requirement.

3. **Check the start date.** If a valid notice is given, the increase cannot take effect in less than 60 days from the notice (under the law in force on 1 October 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Which versions apply:** On 15 October 2026, the current Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). ---

**What the law says**

- You must give the owner (or agent) written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage to the premises [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- You must avoid damaging the premises, and where damage occurs you must notify the rental provider in writing [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Repairs, both urgent and non-urgent, may only be done by a suitably qualified person [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Under section 72, you may arrange urgent repairs only if you have taken reasonable steps to get the owner to do them immediately and you cannot get them done. You must give the owner 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost, and the owner must reimburse the reasonable cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If you don't repair the damage, the owner may give you a repair notice. It must state the damage and that you must repair it within 14 days, or the owner may repair it at your expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This section appears in the earlier version, and the current excerpt cuts off before it, so I can't confirm it is unchanged.
- The Tribunal must consider whether repairs were needed because of the renter's act or omission, and whether the owner was notified and given a reasonable opportunity to repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

**What you can do or ask**

- **Get someone to fix it without telling the owner:** The documents don't support this. Written notice is required [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), and only a suitably qualified person may do the repairs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Skirting boards are probably not urgent, which would mean the non-urgent route applies. That route requires written notice, and the owner must repair within a reasonable time [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Practical next step:** Give the owner written notice now, describing the damage and offering to have it repaired by a suitably qualified tradesperson at your cost or agreed arrangement. Keep photos and receipts. Offering the owner a chance to repair also matters if the Tribunal is later asked to consider the matter [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

**Insurance:** The retrieved documents don't address the owner's insurance, so I can't say whether an unnotified repair would affect it. Check the owner's policy terms or ask the owner or their insurer.

## What the law said on 1 October 2025

- **Inviting higher offers:** A provider or agent must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of rent higher than the advertised amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Accepting unsolicited higher offers:** The version 110 text I retrieved does not contain a ban on *accepting* an unsolicited higher offer. That ban (s 30F(4)) appears in version 111, which took effect on 25 November 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). It does not apply to your situation.
- **Misleading conduct:** A provider or agent must not induce a person to enter an agreement through misleading or deceptive conduct [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This section is about inducing you to *enter* an agreement, and the documents do not clearly say whether a false withdrawal notice falls within it. Section 472(1A) provides for Tribunal orders for contraventions of this section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Discrimination:** A provider must not refuse to let premises on the basis of a protected attribute under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Section 210AA allows a person who has suffered loss from such discrimination to apply to the Tribunal for compensation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

- Your application and any form you were given. Section 30AC requires application forms to be in the prescribed form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The withdrawal email, with full headers, and all other correspondence.
- A note of any phone calls or conversations, including dates, names, and what was said about other offers.

## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110, in force from 6 August 2025** (“rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf”). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A landlord may give a notice to vacate under **section 91ZZB** if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession**. The notice must generally give at least **60 days’ notice** and must include documentary evidence supporting the reason. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The buyer pulling out does **not automatically withdraw** the notice. Under **section 91ZZQ**, a notice to vacate is withdrawn only by a written notice of withdrawal signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

However, the documents do not say that a sale notice remains valid when the proposed sale has fallen through and the premises are no longer going to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession. Therefore, **you may have grounds to challenge its validity**, but the retrieved documents do not establish that the notice is automatically invalid on these facts. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the landlord in writing to confirm whether the property is still being sold or offered for sale with vacant possession, and ask them to give you a **written withdrawal** signed by both sides if it is not. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If the notice was given within the last **30 days**, you may apply to VCAT challenging its validity. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If the landlord applies to VCAT for a possession order, you may challenge the notice on or before the hearing. VCAT decides whether the notice is valid and whether you must leave. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- Do not assume the landlord can physically evict you merely because the notice date has passed: the landlord must obtain a VCAT possession order, and only Victoria Police can carry out a forced eviction under a warrant for possession. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

**So: unless you obtain a valid written withdrawal or VCAT determines that the notice is invalid, the notice has not been withdrawn merely because the buyer pulled out.**

### 1. Requirement to Provide a Washing Machine
Under the *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023* (v002), rooming house operators are legally required to provide at least one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

Yes, operators are permitted to charge for laundry facilities (including via coin-operated machines), but they must follow strict disclosure and pricing rules under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (v115):
* **Private Operators:** If your rooming house is privately owned, the operator can charge you for services like laundry. However, they must give you a separate schedule of these service charges **before** you move in, and if you use the machines, they must provide an itemised account showing your individual use [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Government/Registered Housing:** If your rooming house is managed by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, they can impose a service charge for laundry only if it is not possible to accurately measure your individual use. Even then, the charge cannot exceed the actual cost of providing the service [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 3. What You Can Do or Ask For
* **Request the Schedule:** If you haven't received a schedule of services listing the laundry charges before you moved in, ask your operator for it immediately. They are legally required to provide it prior to your residency [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Check Your Itemised Account:** If you use the coin-operated machines, ask for an itemised account showing exactly how much you have been charged and what that covers [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Verify the Cost:** Ensure the charge per wash does not exceed the actual cost of water and electricity to run the machine. Overcharging for utilities is not permitted under Victorian tenancy law [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

If your operator refuses to provide the required schedule or itemised accounts, or if you believe the charges exceed the actual cost of providing the service, you may apply to the Tribunal to have the charge withdrawn or varied [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Short answer:** Based on the law in force on 1 October 2025, you probably don't have to pay the higher rent yet. A rent increase needs a formal written notice, and an email and a negotiation are not enough.

## What the law says

- **Notice is required.** A rental provider must give at least 60 days' notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The prescribed form is Form 5 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Who gives it.** On Form 5, the rental provider's name "cannot be the agent's name," although the agent's address can be used for service [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The notice should therefore come from the rental provider, not only from the agent.
- **Invalid increases.** "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Other limits.** The notice may provide for only one rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Rent cannot be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Under a fixed-term agreement, rent generally cannot rise during the term unless the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing of payment.** Form 5 says the renter pays the increased amount "from the date provided on this notice unless VCAT decides otherwise" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This only applies if a valid notice has been given.

**Document and version:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 is Version 110, in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 is Version 004, in force from 1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 1 October 2025.

## Applying this to your situation

Your agent's email and the failed negotiation don't appear to meet the notice requirements. Unless you receive a valid Form 5 notice from the rental provider, the documents indicate that no increase is payable. Any increase must also comply with the 60-day notice period, the one-increase limit, and the 12-month interval rule [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for a formal notice.** Request a Form 5 notice from the rental provider that states the current and new rent, the start date, and the method used to calculate the increase [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the timing.** If a valid notice is given, the start date must allow at least 60 days from the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **Challenge it if needed.** If you receive a notice and think the proposed rent is excessive, you can apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You can also apply to VCAT. Under the Act, a renter who has received a notice may apply to VCAT without a Director's report, with leave of the Tribunal, after 30 days from the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Get help.** Form 5 directs renters to the renting section of the Consumer Affairs Victoria website at www.consumer.vic.gov.au/renting or to call 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

A photograph that appears to show mould is **not, by itself, proof** that the premises fail the minimum standard. The standard concerns actual mould or damp and whether it is caused by, or related to, the building structure; the retrieved documents contain no rule saying that a photograph alone proves a breach [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Before applying, ask the provider or agent:

- whether the substance is mould;
- what caused it;
- whether it will be professionally removed and the underlying problem repaired before occupation; and
- for confirmation that the bedroom will meet the minimum standard on the occupation date.

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The buyer pulling out does **not automatically withdraw** the notice. Under section 91ZZQ, a notice is withdrawn only by a written notice of withdrawal signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

However, the notice must be valid, including being in the prescribed form, stating the reason, and—where it is based on sale—being accompanied by approved documentary evidence supporting that reason. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) If the property is no longer going to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession, you may have grounds to challenge whether the notice remains valid; the retrieved documents do not state the precise legal effect of a failed sale.

So, **do not assume you can stay simply because the buyer withdrew**. Unless the landlord formally withdraws the notice, or VCAT determines it is invalid, the notice remains something the landlord may rely on. If you do not leave by the termination date, the landlord may apply to VCAT for a possession order; only Victoria Police can carry out a forced eviction, and only under a warrant based on a VCAT order. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the landlord in writing to withdraw the notice**, using a written withdrawal signed by both of you. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Ask whether the property is still being **offered for sale with vacant possession**, and request the documentary evidence that accompanied the notice. - If you dispute the notice, you may apply to VCAT to challenge its validity **within 30 days after it was given**, and VCAT can determine whether it is valid. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What the law said on 1 March 2023

The applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 002** (in force from 1 June 2022). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved document **does not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits** for a rental. It also does not say that a kettle and heater must be on separate circuits. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

It did require the rental provider to arrange an **electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provided** every **2 years**, conducted by a licensed or registered electrician. The provider must give you the date of the most recent check **in writing if you request it**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The minimum-standard requirement that all power outlets and lighting circuits be connected to a compliant circuit breaker and residual-current device applied **from 29 March 2023**, so it was not yet in force on 1 March 2023. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for

You can write to the rental provider and:

1. **Request, in writing, the date of the most recent electrical safety check.** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
2. Ask them to arrange an electrical safety check if one has not been conducted within the required period. If no check had been conducted within the previous two years when you moved in, the provider had to arrange one **as soon as practicable**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
3. Report that the breaker trips when the kettle and heater operate together, and ask the provider to have the issue investigated by a licensed or registered electrician. The regulations require the provider to maintain the premises in good repair and fit for occupation, but the retrieved documents do not state a specific right to demand an additional circuit or a particular electrical redesign. - **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110**, in force from 6 August 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004**, in force from 1 July 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

A rental provider must give the renter **at least 60 days’ notice, in the prescribed form**, of a proposed rent increase. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The prescribed form says that a valid notice is required for **all** rent increases and must state the current rent, new rent, start date, calculation method and delivery details. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, an ordinary email saying the rent will increase—without the required official notice in the prescribed form—does **not** satisfy the stated notice requirement on the documents provided. A rent increase made in contravention of those requirements is **invalid**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

You therefore do **not** have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed it. The documents do not specify a separate effective date for an invalid increase; on that basis, you should continue paying the current rent rather than the proposed higher amount. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

If a valid notice is later given, the higher rent can begin only from the start date stated in that notice, and the notice must allow at least **60 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) The rent also cannot be increased more than once every **12 months**, and generally cannot be increased during a fixed term unless the agreement permits it in the specified way. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What the law said on 1 November 2019

The applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088** (dated 2 July 2019), which was in force from 2 July to 3 December 2019. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Because you were renting month to month, your agreement was a **periodic tenancy**. A landlord could give a notice to vacate without stating a reason, but the notice had to give at least **120 days’ notice**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

However, such a notice had **no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act**. Asking the landlord to carry out required repairs may be relevant to that protection. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) A challenge to a notice under section 263 had to be made within **60 days after the notice was given**. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf)

Check the notice itself: it must be in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to you, signed by the landlord or agent, and specify the termination date. A notice under section 263 did not have to state a reason. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

For repairs, the Act allowed you to:

- take reasonable steps to arrange **urgent repairs** immediately and, if unsuccessful, arrange the repairs yourself, subject to the Act’s reimbursement rules; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
- if the repairs were **non-urgent**, apply to the Director for an investigation after giving written notice and waiting **14 days** without the repairs being done; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)
- apply to the Tribunal for specified repairs after the Director’s report, or without that report if no report was received within **90 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Record the timing and evidence:** keep your repair requests, photos or videos of the leaking fixtures, replies, dates, the notice, and any statements suggesting the notice was issued because you asked for repairs. The retrieved Act does not prescribe this evidence list, but it is directly relevant to whether the notice was retaliatory under section 266(2). [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Check the 120-day date** and the notice’s form, signature, addressee and termination date. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Consider challenging validity within 60 days** of receiving the notice, relying on section 266(2) if you believe it was retaliation for exercising a statutory repair right. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

4. **Continue pursuing the repairs through the statutory process**: for non-urgent repairs, written notice followed by the Director’s investigation process; for urgent repairs, the urgent-repair provisions. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not state the exact application form or filing procedure for challenging this particular notice, so I cannot specify that procedure from these documents.

**Do you still have to leave?**
Yes. Under Victorian tenancy law, a notice to vacate does not automatically expire or become invalid just because the landlord's reason for giving it (in this case, selling the property) has fallen through. 

**The Law on Withdrawing a Notice**
According to section 91ZZQ of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), a notice to vacate can only be withdrawn if a formal "notice of withdrawal" is given [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This notice of withdrawal must meet strict requirements:
- It must be in writing;
- It must be signed by the landlord (the person who gave the original notice); and
- It must be signed by you, the tenant (the person to whom the notice was given) [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

Because your landlord has not provided this jointly signed notice of withdrawal, your original notice to vacate remains legally valid and in force. You are still bound by the termination date specified in that notice.

**What You Can Do**
1. **Challenge the Notice in VCAT:** If you believe the notice is invalid (for example, because the landlord no longer intends to sell the property), you have the right to apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) to challenge its validity [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Negotiate:** You can ask your landlord to formally withdraw the notice by signing a notice of withdrawal, or negotiate a new agreement, but they are not legally obligated to do so without your consent.

*Note on the applicable law:* The provided documents do not contain a version of the Act explicitly in force on 1 October 2025. However, the rule regarding notice withdrawal under section 91ZZQ is consistent across the versions provided (e.g., Authorised Version v111, effective from November 2025 [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)).
